How to Leave a Cult

There is a technique to leaving a cult. It's in the Rider, Elefant, and Sisyphean chapter. You can rip off the bandage quickly or ease it off gently, but you have to start. Shock and awe are desirable: "Today I quit," just like that. If you think it might help, tell people. Email, group chat, and privacy settings can stage an exit.

You won't get much help from people still in the group, even if they say they are on your side. Think about it: If one person saying no is enough to kill your idea, or make you turn your back on someone, how much do you really trust your group? If your friends fixate on your reactions before and after decisions instead of the decisions themselves, how much can they trust you?

"You can't know them by their friends."

—Proverbs 38:20

Leaving is going to be lonely. You'll meet people outside, and some will know people inside. But you can't control when and how you give the two groups enough context to have a social collision. Don't second-guess when people stay or leave, or what unholy alliance with Satan's minions they have made.

Being around people less immersed in the cult might not be enough to set you free. Immersion is a function of deference, and there's plenty of exuberance in cult fracture. Long-term absence works, if you can stick it out long enough. But you should also start talking to someone who cannot be reached.

TWO MONTHS AGO, THIRTEEN DAYS BEFORE his twelfth birthday, Leo Burnett was dropped off at church—he took guitar, his brother took Bass—and he got there early and went to the bathroom and was washing his hands when the shooter came down the hall and started shooting. The bullets hit the tile and Leo felt them snap the air near his head and he dropped to the floor and crawled out, and later he dreamed for months that he was alive and unhurt but everyone he knew was shot. The nightmares faded, but he still replayed exactly how he'd moved to avoid the bullets.

Leo's church, St. Gabriel's, did everything they could to protect potential shooters from getting guns. They lobbied Washington, D.C., for laws banning assault weapons. They hosted Lock Your Guns Weekends, where people could lock up firearms at the church and get trigger locks and cable locks for free, with rape whistles thrown in. They were planning aletter-writing weekend as part of the March for Our Lives to help teenagers tell lawmakers how they felt. But the gun show loophole grew each year and online gun sales were booming, and angry men with AR-15s posted videos about how much they loved their guns.

The shooter at St. Gabriel's had gotten his weapon through an online ad placed under a stolen identity, and maybe through a gun show or a private seller. Leo couldn't stop thinking about guns and getting them and the trajectories of bullets, and he wrote songs about it, sad and beautiful songs with musical refrains that hurt to listen to. Six weeks after the shooting he played them for his therapist, a man named Jay, and Jay said that it sounded like Leo couldn't stop his mind from replaying exactly where the bullets had gone, as if that might help him dodge the next ones.

Mike sat down beside her and put his arm around her shoulders.

"I think so," he said.

And they watched the stars come out until their wine was gone.

The Bauers did not take down the ramp. Nor did they pay the fine. Instead they sued the homeowners' association on Emma's behalf. And in May, 2005 — eight months after the ramp first went up — a jury in the state courthouse awarded Emma and her parents $25,000 in damages, the maximum allowed by law. This summer the HOA agreed to pay the Bauers' court costs as well.

As you might guess, this story's been written up in newspapers and magazine s around the country. It's become an often-cited example of how federal disability law, broadly interpreted by the courts, is forcing American neighborhoods to change. It's also become a rallying cry for outraged homeowners on both coasts. The Bauers, locals claim, are representative of a new and especially heartless breed of handicapped person — the one who demands the right to park in every possible space, who rides into Starbucks and blocks the door, who insists on a ramp up every single step and who must beamage, lives woodsacre in lawsuits to get his way.

Not long ago I called Gary Pfeiffer at his home to ask him if he had any regrets. The ice cream coupon was only a PR maneuver, he told me.

"I don't think it was the right thing to do," he said. "It was the wrong thing to do, but you do it because you want to be a nice guy."

That Sunday, with Emma at the kitchen table working on her spelling, Kate pored over the code books until she found the section that dealt with ramps. The height of the handrails had to be between twenty-eight and thirty-four inches. The landing had to be at least five by five. The slope had to be less than one-twelve. None of these measurements was met by their new ramp. The city did not allow building permit applications to be filed on Sundays.

Nonetheless, the next Saturday morning, Mike stood on ladders with his brother as Kate hammered stakes into the ground to mark where the new ramp would go. It rose at a slightly different angle, long enough to reach the doorframe, with landings at either end and a smooth metal rail. When they were done, Mike took Emma in her chair to the bottom of it and told her to give it a try. The first time, her wheels caught on the corners of the landing, and Mike had to catch her, but by the third try she was rolling up easily.

She started a petition. It had a simple request: reconsideration of the decision in the Bauer case, with the possibility of amending the bylaws regarding accessibility. It included a paragraph about community spirit and neighbors helping neighbors.

Within three days, she had 120 signatures - every house on their street, and then some. People she didn't even know were stopping by. Mrs. Whitcomb even signed! 

At the next board meeting, Kate handed Gary the petition. "This isn't just about a ramp," she said, her voice shaking only slightly. "It's about what we value as a community. It's about making Willow Creek a place where everyone belongs."

Gary looked at the petition. He looked at Emma. He opened his mouth to speak, then closed it. He looked at the other board members, and smiled slightly. 

He cleared his throat. "I have a motion," he said. "We amend the bylaws to allow for reasonable accommodations for residents with disabilities, specifically including ramps and other accessibility features.  Second?"

The motion passed unanimously. Kate went to Emma, and hugged her tightly.  A neighbor said, "Well, it's about time."  

Later that evening, Kate found Gary in his yard, pruning roses. "Thank you," she said.

He shrugged. "I'm an accountant," he said, smile twisting a little. "I deal with rules. But sometimes...sometimes the rules need to change." He paused and looked at the ramp. “My mother used a wheelchair for the last ten years of her life." He didn't meet Kate's eyes, but she understood.

Kate nodded and closed the space between them. "It makes all the difference, doesn't it?"

Gary looked at the ramp, then back at Kate. "Yes," he said quietly. "It truly does."

The Bauers, a couple with a nine-year-old girl named Emma, who had to use a wheelchair due to a car accident in March. They couldn't, however, afford to remake their house, but Emma's dad, Mike, and his brother, built a wooden ramp up to the entrance: thirty feet long, with two switchbacks and a railing, coloured to match the porch. It took them three weekends in total.

Just two weeks later the Willow Creek Homeowners Association sent them a letter. The rules forbid "permanent structures in front yards," and a neighbour had informed them. The ramp needed to be taken down within sixty days, or the Bauers would be fined $100 a day.

Kate begged the committee for an exception. The neighbour who had filed a complaint, Mrs. Whitcomb next door, suggested a ramp through the garage instead. But that would mean Emma went into the own house past the trash cans and the furnace, through a door that got stuck, and Emma had cried when they discussed it.

At the board meeting on Tuesday, at the clubhouse, the four other members split two to two. That left the president, Gary Pfeiffer, a retired accountant who had been on the board for eleven years and was known for following the rules. He had asked careful questions all night and given no hint which way he will vote. Emma sat in her chair at the end of the second row besides her mother.

Gary looked at his notes, then at the Bauers. "I've thought about this a lot," he said. "I'm voting to deny the exception, for two reasons. One, it affects property values. And two, if we let you have a ramp, what's next? Parking in the front yard for emergencies? Chicken coops?"
